---
title: "Singular mixed model fits"
---

The [random-effects-correlation page](random-effect-correlations.qmd) represented intercept and slope deviations with a covariance matrix. A [**singular fit**](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/isSingular.html) occurs when the estimated random-effects covariance matrix has lower rank than the model specification allows.

A singularity warning concerns the rank of the fitted covariance matrix. A convergence warning concerns the numerical search used to fit the model.

## Beginning with a two dimensional structure

Suppose a model includes listener random intercepts and noise slopes:

```r
log_rt ~ noise_condition +
  (1 + noise_condition | listener)
```

The listener covariance matrix is

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\tau_0^2 & \rho\tau_0\tau_1\\
\rho\tau_0\tau_1 & \tau_1^2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

With positive intercept and slope variances and a correlation inside the interval $(-1,1)$, the matrix has rank two. It represents two directions of group variation.

If $\widehat\tau_1=0$, the slope direction collapses. The model requested between-group slope variation, but the fitted covariance matrix contains none. If $|\widehat\rho|=1$, one deviation is a perfect linear function of the other, and the matrix again loses a dimension.

In either case, the fitted random-effect covariance matrix has lost a dimension and is singular.

## Separating singularity from nonconvergence

An optimizer can converge successfully to a boundary value while the fitted covariance matrix is singular. Software may thus report successful convergence and a singularity warning for the same fit.

The reverse is also possible. An estimated covariance matrix can be nonsingular even though the optimizer failed to settle at a reliable optimum. That fit receives a convergence warning without a singularity warning.

Both checks are needed:

```r
isSingular(fit_correlated, tol = 1e-4)
summary(fit_correlated)
```

The first command checks the rank of the fitted covariance matrix. The summary and optimizer messages report whether the numerical search converged.

## Inspecting the design before changing the model

A random slope requires within group predictor variation. If many listeners appear in only one condition, the design cannot separate their baselines from listener specific condition associations. Few listener levels or few observations per condition can also leave the slope variance weakly informed.

The same reasoning applies to crossed item slopes. A condition that varies within listeners but not within items may support a listener slope and fail to support an item slope.

Thus a singular fit should send us back to the sources of dependence and the within-group predictor support. The first question is not which term makes a warning disappear. It is which requested population variation the design can identify.

## Inspecting the fitted dimensions

`rePCA()` rotates the estimated covariance matrix into independent directions and reports their standard deviations:

```r
rePCA(fit_correlated)
```

In a larger random effects structure, individual variances and correlations may not reveal the collapsed combination. The rotated representation can show that one linear combination of deviations has an estimated standard deviation near zero.

When a formula has several slopes, the singularity may involve a combination of them rather than one variance component equal to zero. The rotated standard deviations help identify that combination.

## Revising the population model deliberately

After inspecting the design and fitted covariance matrix, consider the following responses.

1. removing an unsupported correlation while retaining both variances;
2. removing a slope variance that the design cannot identify;
3. collecting more levels or within group contrasts;
4. using a regularized model that retains uncertainty near the boundary.

These responses do not make the same assumption. Removing the correlation sets the intercept-slope correlation to zero. Removing a slope sets its between-group variance to zero. Collecting more data retains the richer population model while changing the design.

Do not simplify solely to obtain a smaller standard error or a preferred significance result. The random effects structure encodes the populations across which the comparison should generalize.

## Reporting the resolution

A singular-fit report should answer four questions:

1. the original random effects specification;
2. the diagnostic showing singularity;
3. the revised specification and its design justification;
4. whether the population comparison changes materially.

The singular fit is evidence about the relation between the requested covariance structure and the available data. Hiding the warning loses that evidence. Treating every singular fit as proof that group variation is exactly zero overstates it.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the dimensions"}
A model converges but estimates its random slope standard deviation as zero. Which diagnostic has failed? What design property would you inspect before removing the slope?
:::
